## Problem 1 
```{r}
#### Load data here and libraries
library(tidyverse)
library(p8105.datasets)
data("ny_noaa")


#### Summary calculations and get data prepared
n_obs = nrow(ny_noaa)
n_cols = ncol(ny_noaa)
n_stations = ny_noaa |> 
  pull(id) |> 
  n_distinct()


#### Consider percentages and counts to summarize
total_record_count = nrow(ny_noaa)
total_column_count = ncol(ny_noaa)
total_distinct_stations = ny_noaa |> 
  summarize(n = n_distinct(id)) |> 
  pull(n)


#### Missing data percentages (`NA`)
pct_missing_tmax = ny_noaa |> 
  summarize(pct = mean(is.na(tmax)) * 100) |> 
  pull(pct)
pct_missing_tmin = ny_noaa |> 
  summarize(pct = mean(is.na(tmin)) * 100) |> 
  pull(pct)
pct_missing_prcp = ny_noaa |> 
  summarize(pct = mean(is.na(prcp)) * 100) |> 
  pull(pct)
pct_missing_snow = ny_noaa |> 
  summarize(pct = mean(is.na(snow)) * 100) |> 
  pull(pct)
pct_missing_snwd = ny_noaa |> 
  summarize(pct = mean(is.na(snwd)) * 100) |> 
  pull(pct)
```


### Problem 1.1: Short description of the dataset
The `ny_noaa` dataset has weather observations collected from New York State (NYS) weather stations between 1981 and 2010. There are 2,595,176 observations and `r ncol(ny_noaa)` variables included: station ID (`id`), observation date (`date`), precipitation (`prcp`, in tenths of mm), snowfall (`snow`, in mm), snow depth (`snwd`, in mm), and daily max and min temperatures (`tmax` and `tmin`, in tenths of degrees C). Missing data is an issue here because stations sometimes collected a subset of variables rather than all of the variables. For instance, `tmax` is missing in `r round(mean(is.na(ny_noaa$tmax)) * 100, 1)`% of observations and `tmin` is missing in `r round(mean(is.na(ny_noaa$tmin)) * 100, 1)`%.


```{r}
#### Clean variables and convert units for ease
ny_noaa_clean = 
  ny_noaa |> 
  janitor::clean_names() |> 
  separate(date, into = c("year", "month", "day"), 
           sep = "-", convert = TRUE) |> 
  mutate(
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax) / 10,
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin) / 10,
    prcp = prcp / 10
  )


#### Find 10 most common snowfall values across NYS 1981-2010
common_snowfall_values = 
  ny_noaa_clean |> 
  janitor::tabyl(snow) |> 
  arrange(desc(n)) |> 
  slice(1:10)
```


### Problem 1.2: The why?
I cleaned the variable names using janitor::clean_names(), then separated the date variable into integer columns for year, month, and day. Maximum temp. (`tmax`), minimum temp. (`tmin`), and prec. (`prcp`) were divided by 10 to converted from tenths of units into Celsius (C) and millimeters (mm). Looking at the 10 most common snowfall values, `0mm` is by far the most frequent since it doesn't snow in NYS more than it is. Missing data, `NA`, is the second most common in the data, which makes sense because a lot of weather stations don't collect or report snowfall especially in the summer, for instance. After `0` and `NA`, smaller values like 3mm and 5mm in the top ten could be due to measurement differences across stations because some stations recording trace amounts or using direct measurements.


```{r}
#### Calculate the average tmax in January and in July per station and year
jan_jul_df = 
  ny_noaa_clean |> 
  filter(month == 1 | month == 7) |> 
  group_by(id, year, month) |> 
  summarize(mean_tmax = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE))


#### Plot January-July snowfall in NYS
ggplot(jan_jul_df, aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax, group = id)) + 
  geom_line(alpha = 0.5) + 
  facet_wrap(~ month) +
  labs(
    title = "Average Max. Temp. in January and July in NYS from 1981 and 2010",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Average Max Temperature (C)"
  )
```

### Problem 1.3: Patterns and outliers
These two figures show a clear pattern that max. temps are consistently lower in January and much higher in July. There are a few noticeable outliers across the years, such as an unusually cold January ~1998 where temperatures dropped below the other years and a cold July ~1987. There also seemed to be a very warm July in 2010. While some outliers could be due to localized weather events, measurement errors at stations or between workers, and broader climate patterns (e.g., climate change) highlight the variability in NYS temperatures across time.


```{r}
#### tmax vs tmin plot using ggplot
ny_noaa_clean |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = tmin, y = tmax)) +
  geom_bin_2d(bins = 50) +
    scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "K") +
  labs(
    title = "Daily Minimum and Maximum Temperatures in NYS (1981-2010)",
    x = "Minimum Temperature (C)",
    y = "Maximum Temperature (C)",
    fill = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1),
    legend.position = "none",
    legend.key.width = unit(1.5, "cm"),
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold", size = 14)
  )
```


```{r}
#### Distribution of snowfall  by year
ny_noaa_clean |> 
  filter(snow > 0 & snow < 100) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(year), y = snow, fill = as.numeric(year))) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "K") +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Snowfall (0-100 mm) in NYS, 1981-2010",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Snowfall (mm)",
    fill = "Year"
  ) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold", size = 14)
  )
```


## Problem 2
```{r}
#### Load demographic data
covar_df = 
  read_csv("https://p8105.com/data/nhanes_covar.csv", 
           skip = 4) |> 
  janitor::clean_names() |> 
  filter(age >= 21) |> 
  drop_na(sex, age, bmi, education) |> 
  mutate(
    sex = factor(
      sex, 
      levels = c(1, 2), 
      labels = c("Male", "Female")
    ),
    education = factor(
      education, 
      levels = c(1, 2, 3), 
      labels = c("Less than high school", 
                 "High school equivalent", 
                 "More than high school"),
      ordered = TRUE
    )
  )


#### Load accelerometer data next
accel_df = 
  read_csv("https://p8105.com/data/nhanes_accel.csv") |> 
  janitor::clean_names()


#### Merge these datasets!
nhanes_df = 
  inner_join(covar_df, accel_df, by = "seqn")
```


```{r}
#### Ages for men-women (sex) across educational attainment in NHANES
nhanes_df |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = sex, y = age, fill = sex)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.6, outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~ education) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("Male" = "#2B5C9D", "Female" = "#E86A8A")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Age Distribution by Sex Across Levels of Education Among NHANES Participants",
    x = "Sex",
    y = "Age",
    fill = "Sex"
  ) +
theme_classic() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold", size = 14)
  )
```


### Problem 2.1: Explanation/comment
Across education levels, overall sample sizes remain highest in the "More than high school" category. But participant counts are roughly equal between men and women. The plot shows demographic trends also: participants in the "More than high school" category skew younger overall, whereas those in the "Less than high school" category skew older. Sex differences in age distribution are most pronounced in the "High school equivalent" category, where female participants are noticeably older on average compared to male participants, who skew younger.


```{r}
#### Aggregate MIMS to calculate total daily activity
nhanes_total_act = 
  nhanes_df |> 
  mutate(total_activity = rowSums(across(starts_with("min"))))


#### Plot activity against age by sex x education levels
nhanes_total_act |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = age, y = total_activity, color = sex)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ education) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("Male" = "#2B5C9D", "Female" = "#E86A8A")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Total Daily Activity vs. Age by Sex Across Educational Attainment Among NHANES Participants",
    x = "Age (Years)",
    y = "Total Daily Activity (MIMS)",
    color = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold", size = 12)
  )
```

### Problem 2.2: Explanation/comment
Total daily physical activity generally declines as age increases across three levels of educational attainment. Also generally speaking, female participants exhibit greater average total activity levels compared to male participants, a difference that is most noticeable in the "High school equivalent" and "More than high school" tiers across middle age. 



```{r}
# Pivot MIMS and convert units
nhanes_time_course = 
  nhanes_df |> 
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("min"),
    names_to = "minute",
    names_prefix = "min",
    values_to = "mims"
  ) |> 
  mutate(minute = as.numeric(minute))


#### Plot showing 24-hour activity time by education level x sex
nhanes_time_course |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = minute / 60, y = mims, color = sex)) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE, linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ education) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Male" = "#2B5C9D", "Female" = "#E86A8A")) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = c(0, 6, 12, 18, 24),
    labels = c("12 AM", "6 AM", "12 PM", "6 PM", "12 AM"),
    limits = c(0, 24),
    expand = c(0, 0.5)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "24-Hour Activity Level by Education and Sex",
    x = "Time of Day",
    y = "Activity (MIMS)",
    color = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold", size = 14)
  )
```


### Problem 2.3: Explanation/comment
The plots show patterns in physical activity (or MIMS) across education levels and sex. Across all groups, activity follows circadian rhythm cycles, dropping to zero or very little between midnight and 6 AM to reflect sleep windows. Females demonstrate slightly higher mean activity levels than males across all educational levels. Additionally, individuals with less than a high school education exhibit higher overall peak activity during midday compared to those with high school equivalents or post-secondary education.



## Problem 3
```{r}
#### Read all 4 CSV files
file_paths <- 
  list.files(pattern = "\\.csv$", ignore.case = TRUE, full.names = TRUE)

#### Import and clean data
citibike_df <- read_csv(file_paths, id = "file_name") |> 
  clean_names() |> 
  mutate(
    ###### Include months
    month = if_else(str_detect(file_name, "(?i)jan"), "January", "July"),
    month = factor(month, levels = c("January", "July")),

    ##### Include year
    year = if_else(str_detect(file_name, "2020"), "2020", "2024"),
    year = factor(year),

    ##### Include days
    weekdays = factor(
      weekdays, 
      levels = c("Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday", "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday")
    ),
    rideable_type = factor(
      rideable_type, 
      levels = c("classic_bike", "electric_bike"),
      labels = c("Classic Bike", "Electric Bike")
    ),
    member_casual = factor(
      member_casual, 
      levels = c("casual", "member"),
      labels = c("Casual", "Member")
    )
  ) |> 
  select(-file_name)


ride_summary

```

### Problem 3.1: Description of data
This df merges Citi Bike data from four time periods: January 2020, July 2020, January 2024, and July 2024. The df contains 99,485 bike rides across 10 columns, including the trip identifiers, trip duration, starting and ending station names, and other details like the day of the week, month, and year.


```{r}
# Creating table
ride_summary <- citibike_df |> 
  group_by(year, month, member_casual) |> 
  summarize(total_rides = n(), .groups = "drop") |> 
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = member_casual,
    values_from = total_rides
  ) |> 
  mutate(Total = Casual + Member)
```



### Problem 3.2: July 2024 data
```{r}
#### Create July 2024 table with top stations
top_5_start_stations_jul_2024 <- 
  citibike_df |> 
  filter(year == "2024", month %in% c("Jul", "July")) |> 
  count(start_station_name, name = "number_of_rides", sort = TRUE) |> 
  slice_head(n = 5) |> 
  rename(
    `Starting Station` = start_station_name,
    `Number of Rides` = number_of_rides
  )

top_5_start_stations_jul_2024
```

#### Problem 3.3: Effects of timing on median ride duration
```{r}
#### Calculate median duration by year, month, and day of week
weekdays = factor(
  weekdays, 
  levels = c("Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday", "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday")
)
median_duration_df <- 
  citibike_df |> 
  group_by(year, month, day_of_week) |> 
  summarize(median_duration = median(duration, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

##### Create multi-panel line plot for easy comparison across all 3 variables
ggplot(median_duration_df, aes(x = day_of_week, y = median_duration, group = month, color = month)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  facet_wrap(~ year) +
  labs(
    title = "Median Ride Duration by Day of Week, Month, and Year",
    x = "Day of the Week",
    y = "Median Duration (Minutes)",
    color = "Month"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14)
  )
```
